paragraphs: Before we examine any other objections to an indefinite power of taxation in the Union, I shall make one general remark. If the national government's jurisdiction over revenue were restricted to particular objects, an undue share of the public burdens would naturally fall on those objects. Two evils would spring from this: the oppression of particular branches of industry, and an unequal distribution of the taxes, both among the individual States and among the citizens of the same State.

Suppose, as has been argued, that the federal power of taxation were confined to duties on imports. It is evident that the government, unable to command other resources, would often be tempted to push these duties to an injurious excess. Some people imagine that such duties can never be carried too far. The higher they are, it is alleged, the more they will discourage extravagant consumption, produce a favorable balance of trade and promote domestic manufactures. But every extreme is harmful in various ways. Exorbitant duties on imported articles would breed a general spirit of smuggling, which always harms the fair trader and in the end the revenue itself. They tend to make other classes of the community tributary, to an improper degree, to the manufacturing classes, to whom they give a premature monopoly of the markets. They sometimes force industry out of its more natural channels into others where it flows with less advantage. And finally, they oppress the merchant, who is often obliged to pay them himself with no repayment from the consumer. When demand matches the quantity of goods at market, the consumer generally pays the duty. But when the markets happen to be overstocked, a great share falls on the merchant, and sometimes it not only eats up his profits but cuts into his capital. I am inclined to think that the duty is divided between seller and buyer more often than is commonly imagined. It is not always possible to raise the price of a commodity in exact proportion to each additional imposition laid on it. The merchant, especially in a country with a small commercial capital, is often forced to hold prices down so as to sell more quickly.

The maxim that the consumer is the payer holds so much more often than its opposite that it is far more equitable for the duties on imports to go into a common stock than to benefit the importing States alone. But the maxim is not true often enough to make it equitable for those duties to be the only national fund. When the merchant pays them, they work as an additional tax on the importing State, whose citizens pay their share as consumers. In this way they produce inequality among the States, and the inequality would grow as the duties grew. Confining the national revenues to this kind of impost would also produce inequality, from a different cause, between the manufacturing and the non-manufacturing States. The States that can go furthest in supplying their own wants from their own manufactures will not, in proportion to their numbers or wealth, consume as large a share of imported articles as the States that are not so favorably placed. By this means alone, then, they would not contribute to the public treasury in proportion to their abilities. To make them do so, we must have recourse to excises, whose proper objects are particular kinds of manufactures. New York has a deeper interest in these considerations than those of her citizens who argue for limiting the power of the Union to external taxation may realize. New York is an importing State and is not likely soon to become, to any great extent, a manufacturing State. She would therefore suffer in two ways from confining the Union's jurisdiction to commercial imposts.

These observations are meant to show a danger that the import duties might be pushed to an injurious extreme. On that point, as I remarked in another part of these papers, the interest of the revenue itself would be a sufficient guard against such an extreme. I readily admit this would be so as long as other resources were open. But if the avenues to them were closed, HOPE, spurred by necessity, would produce experiments, backed by rigorous precautions and additional penalties. These would have the intended effect for a time, until people had leisure to devise ways around the new precautions. The first success would be apt to inspire false opinions, which might take a long course of later experience to correct. Necessity, especially in politics, often gives rise to false hopes, false reasonings, and a correspondingly mistaken system of measures. But even if this supposed excess should not result from limiting the federal power of taxation, the inequalities I have described would still follow, though not to the same degree, from the other causes I have noted. Let us now return to examining objections.

One objection, which to judge by how often it is repeated seems the one most relied on, is that the House of Representatives is not numerous enough to take in all the different classes of citizens, so as to combine the interests and feelings of every part of the community and to produce a due sympathy between the representative body and its constituents. This argument comes in a very specious and seductive form and is well designed to seize on the prejudices of those it is addressed to. But when we dissect it with attention, it turns out to be made up of nothing but fair-sounding words. The object it seems to aim at is, in the first place, impracticable, and in the sense in which it is urged, unnecessary. I reserve for another place the question whether the representative body is sufficient in numbers. Here I shall content myself with examining the particular use that has been made of the contrary supposition in connection with the subject of our present inquiries.

The idea of actual representation of all classes of the people by persons from each class is altogether visionary. Unless the Constitution expressly provided that each different occupation should send one or more members, the thing would never happen in practice. Mechanics and manufacturers will always be inclined, with few exceptions, to vote for merchants rather than for persons of their own professions or trades. These discerning citizens are well aware that the mechanic and manufacturing arts furnish the materials of mercantile enterprise and industry. Many of them, indeed, are directly connected with the operations of commerce. They know that the merchant is their natural patron and friend. They know that, however much confidence they may rightly have in their own good sense, the merchant can advance their interests more effectively than they can themselves. They are aware that their habits in life have not given them those acquired endowments without which, in a deliberative assembly, the greatest natural abilities are for the most part useless. And they are aware that the influence, weight and superior acquirements of the merchants make them better able to contend with any spirit that might happen to find its way into the public councils unfriendly to the manufacturing and trading interests. These considerations, and many others that might be mentioned, prove, and experience confirms, that artisans and manufacturers will commonly be disposed to give their votes to merchants and to those whom the merchants recommend. We must therefore consider merchants the natural representatives of all these classes of the community.

As for the learned professions, little needs to be said. They truly form no distinct interest in society, and depending on their situation and talents, they will be chosen, without distinction, by each other and by other parts of the community, as the objects of their confidence.

Nothing remains but the landed interest. In a political view, and particularly with respect to taxes, I take this to be perfectly united, from the wealthiest landlord down to the poorest tenant. No tax can be laid on land that will not affect the owner of millions of acres just as it affects the owner of a single acre. Every landholder will therefore share an interest in keeping the taxes on land as low as possible, and common interest can always be counted on as the surest bond of sympathy. But even if we could suppose a difference of interest between the wealthy landholder and the middling farmer, what reason is there to conclude that the first would have a better chance than the last of being sent to the national legislature? If we take fact as our guide and look at our own senate and assembly, we shall find that moderate landowners prevail in both. This is no less true in the senate, which has fewer members, than in the assembly, which has more. Where the qualifications of the electors are the same, whether they have to choose a small number or a large one, their votes will go to those in whom they have most confidence, whether these happen to be men of large fortunes, of moderate property, or of no property at all.

It is said to be necessary that every class of citizens have some of its own number in the representative body, so that its feelings and interests may be better understood and attended to. But we have seen that this will never happen under any arrangement that leaves the votes of the people free. Where they are free, the representative body will be composed of landholders, merchants and men of the learned professions, with too few exceptions to have any influence on the spirit of the government. But where is the danger that these three kinds of men will fail to understand or attend to the interests and feelings of the different classes of citizens? Will not the landholder know and feel whatever will promote or secure the interest of landed property? Will he not, from his own stake in that kind of property, be inclined enough to resist every attempt to harm or burden it? Will not the merchant understand, and be disposed to cultivate as far as is proper, the interests of the mechanic and manufacturing arts, to which his commerce is so closely allied? And will not the man of a learned profession, who will feel neutral toward the rivalries between the different branches of industry, be likely to prove an impartial arbiter between them, ready to promote either so far as it seems to him to serve the general interests of society?

Now take into account the passing moods or dispositions that may happen to prevail in particular parts of society, and to which a wise administration will never be inattentive. Is a man whose situation leads him to wide inquiry and information less likely to judge their nature, extent and foundation competently than a man whose observation does not go beyond the circle of his neighbors and acquaintances? Is it not natural that a man who is a candidate for the favor of the people, and who depends on the votes of his fellow citizens to keep his public honors, should take care to inform himself of their dispositions and inclinations and should be willing to allow them their proper degree of influence on his conduct? This dependence, and the necessity of binding himself and his posterity by the laws to which he gives his assent, are the true and strong chords of sympathy between the representative and the constituent.

Of all the business of government, taxation demands the most extensive information and the most thorough knowledge of the principles of political economy. A man who understands those principles best will be the least likely to turn to oppressive expedients, or to sacrifice some particular class of citizens in order to raise revenue. It could be demonstrated that the most productive system of finance is always the least burdensome. There can be no doubt that anyone who is to exercise the power of taxation judiciously must know the general character, habits and ways of thinking of the people at large, and must know the resources of the country. That is all anyone can reasonably mean by a knowledge of the interests and feelings of the people. In any other sense the claim means nothing, or something absurd. Taking it in that sense, let every considerate citizen judge for himself where the needed qualification is most likely to be found.
